Glossary

    Examples · Pro

    Words: 1090

    Seven techniques for the “my scripts run on other people's machines” level. The goal of this level is to eliminate silent failures: whatever can go wrong must report it out loud.

    Key idea of this page #

    The difference between Noob and Pro is not command recall, but the approach to failure. A beginner scripts the happy path; a professional assumes commands will fail, network connections will flap, and the script will be executed twice concurrently or interrupted mid-run. The seven techniques below target precisely these realities: loud failures with line numbers, guaranteed temporary file cleanup, non-destructive dry-run modes, bounded retries, bounded concurrency with error aggregation, single-instance execution locks, and logging that does not pollute data streams. None of them are complex. What is difficult is remembering them before an incident occurs, rather than after.

    1 · Failing loudly: trap ERR with line numbers #

    Task: Ensure a failing script automatically reports where the failure occurred.

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

on_err() {
  local rc=$?
  echo "FAILURE: line $1, exit code $rc" >&2
  exit "$rc"
}
trap 'on_err $LINENO' ERR
    Why so: Bash lacks native call stacks on failure, so reporting the exact line number of an error is the only diagnostic clue to help you localize crashes. Always specify the -E option: without it, your ERR trap is never inherited by functions or subshells, and internal function errors bypass your handler entirely. Store the exit status via local rc=$? as the first instruction: any intermediate command will overwrite the failure code.

    2 · Temporary directory guaranteed to clean up #

    Task: Process intermediate files leaving zero debris on error or Ctrl+C.

    tmp=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/app.XXXXXX")
cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmp"; }
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

work > "$tmp/out"
mv "$tmp/out" result.txt
    Why so: An EXIT trap reliably executes upon any termination of your script (including abrupt exits under set -e), except uncatchable SIGKILL which the kernel handles directly. Trapping INT and TERM ensures cleanup handlers run when users interrupt execution. Always delegate temporary naming to mktemp rather than inventing paths yourself: predictable names in shared /tmp create race conditions and symlink vulnerabilities. Move completed artifacts to their destination atomically so readers never observe partial files.

    3 · Command options and mandatory --dry-run #

    Task: Equip a script with options and a “show what would happen without executing” mode.

    dry=0; verbose=0
while getopts ":nvh" opt; do
  case $opt in
    n) dry=1 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    h) usage; exit 0 ;;
    \?) echo "unknown option" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))

run() { (( dry )) && { echo "DRY: $*"; return 0; }; "$@"; }
run rm -rf "$target"
    Why so: A leading colon in your optstring places getopts into silent mode, letting you handle errors programmatically. Running shift $((OPTIND - 1)) strips parsed options so that $1 points directly to your first positional argument. The run wrapper bakes dry-run mode directly into your script architecture: route destructive commands through it so you never forget to respect --dry-run. Watch out for the redirection trap: the shell evaluates output operators before entering functions, meaning run echo x > file truncates file even during simulation because > has already executed. Wrap mutations inside subshells like run sh -c 'echo x > file' or isolate them in functions that verify dry-run status internally.

    4 · Retries with exponential backoff #

    Task: Survive transient network hiccups without degenerating into an infinite loop.

    retry() {
  local n=0 max=5 delay=1
  until "$@"; do
    n=$((n + 1))
    (( n >= max )) && return 1
    sleep "$delay"
    delay=$((delay * 2))
  done
}

retry curl -fsS --max-time 10 "$url"
    Why so: Protect retry loops from infinite hanging with three safeguards: attempt limits, exponential backoff, and a command-level timeout. Without --max-time, your script will freeze on the very first stalled connection and retries will never trigger. Always pass -f to curl: without it, HTTP 500 responses are treated as successes, preventing your loop from detecting the outage.

    5 · Bounded parallel processing with error aggregation #

    Task: Process a hundred files across four parallel workers and verify if any failed.

    export -f process          # visible in xargs

printf '%s\0' logs/*.log \
  | xargs -0 -P4 -I{} bash -c 'process "$@"' _ {} \
  || echo "some tasks failed" >&2

# manual tracking with exit codes:
pids=(); for f in logs/*.log; do work "$f" & pids+=($!); done
rc=0; for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p" || rc=1; done
    Why so: When processing batches in parallel, null terminators via \0 and the -0 flag safeguard your pipeline against spaces and newlines in filenames. xargs returns a non-zero exit status if even a single worker fails - providing reliable failure aggregation that backgrounding with & and wait lacks. If you need individual exit codes per file, preserve PIDs using $! and wait on each worker explicitly.

    6 · Single instance: protecting against concurrent runs #

    Task: Prevent a cron job from starting a second instance if the previous run is still active.

    exec 9>/var/lock/app.lock
flock -n 9 || { echo "already running" >&2; exit 0; }

# subsequent standard execution
    Why so: An flock lock is bound to an open file descriptor, not a filesystem path: the kernel automatically releases it when your process terminates, even during unhandled panics. Ad-hoc lock files lack this property: a crashed process leaves stale locks behind, permanently blocking your subsequent runs. The -n flag requests non-blocking checks; exiting with code 0 is deliberate here so cron never inundates you with false alerts on skipped runs.

    7 · Leveled logging #

    Task: Provide diagnostic logging that does not corrupt command stdout.

    LOG_LEVEL="${LOG_LEVEL:-info}"
_log() {
  local lvl=$1; shift
  printf '%s [%s] %s\n' \
    "$(date -Is)" "$lvl" "$*" >&2
}
info() { [ "$LOG_LEVEL" = debug ] || [ "$LOG_LEVEL" = info ] && _log INFO "$@"; }
die()  { _log ERROR "$@"; exit 1; }
    Why so: Always stream log messages from your script to stderr: standard output (stdout) is reserved for data consumed by downstream pipeline commands. Format timestamps with -Is (ISO 8601) so lines sort lexicographically and parsers process dates without regular expressions. Read log levels from environment variables: this allows you to toggle verbosity in production without modifying deployed scripts.

    Artifacts: what you take away from this page #

    Reading >> Your life quantum · Dignity partnership with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    Seven modular patterns and the exact failures each defends against. Your time was well spent if when drafting your next script you reflexively ask “what happens if this crashes midway through” - and already know the solution. That is the essence of rewiring: failure handling stops being an afterthought and becomes an integral part of design.

    1. set -Eeuo pipefail and trap ERR $LINENO - failures name their exact location.
    2. mktemp -d with trap EXIT INT TERM - guaranteed cleanup on all exits except kill -9.
    3. getopts and the run wrapper - architectural dry-run checks and internal redirection.
    4. Bounded retries with timeouts, and why curl -f is mandatory.
    5. xargs -0 -P - safe filenames and aggregated exit status reporting.
    6. Descriptor-based flock instead of brittle pid-files.
    7. Stderr logging with environment-driven log levels.
